## What I found

No. The subject is a `StorageProvider` interface over the only S3 client, proposed so a vendor swap would be easier later. The verdict is **drop it (the record calls this DROP on a necessity failure)** — the deciding fact is the one you gave: there is no second store planned or requested, so the interface would ship with exactly one implementation and the variation it exists to absorb has no date, no requester, and no constraint behind it. That is §1a *generality without instantiation*, and the port/strategy pattern's prerequisite — two or more implementations — does not hold. The optionality premium in §8a only applies to a *named, probable* next implementation; "some vendor, someday" is the speculative case it explicitly excludes.

One thing that is not settled by this answer: if the real pain is that S3 types and bucket/key strings are spreading into business logic, or that tests need a seam, that is a *different* problem from vendor portability and earns its own evidence. It would justify a narrow function or two named in your domain's terms (`store_upload`, `fetch_upload`), not a vendor-neutral provider abstraction. Decide that on call-site duplication you can point at, not on portability.

## Why it matters

Acting on the proposal costs an indirection layer, a second naming vocabulary for every storage concept, and a lowest-common-denominator API that silently drops the S3 features you do use — presigned URLs, multipart, storage classes, conditional writes — because a hypothetical competitor might not have them. That tax is paid on every storage change from now on. Not acting costs you nothing today: the day a real second vendor arrives, you will extract the interface from working code and known call sites, which is cheaper and produces a better interface than guessing the seam now. A vendor migration is dominated by data transfer, consistency semantics, and IAM, none of which an interface solves.

## Do this first

1. Call the AWS SDK directly from the code that needs storage, and reject the proposal in whatever record your team keeps (issue or ADR) with the structural rationale — "one implementation, no second store named" — so it is not re-proposed without new evidence.
2. If S3 details are leaking into domain logic, grep your call sites for `boto3`/`S3Client`/bucket-name literals; if more than a handful of modules hold them, introduce a thin domain-named module over the SDK, with S3 types in the signatures and no pretense of vendor neutrality.
3. Revisit automatically if a second store is actually named — a contract, a region/compliance requirement, or an on-prem deployment — at which point extract the interface from the two real call patterns.

## What I did not check

- Your actual call sites and whether S3 details already leak into domain code: `rg -n "boto3|S3Client|aws-sdk|@aws-sdk/client-s3|s3://" --stats` in the repo root. This directory contains only the skill library (`.claude/skills/`), no application code, so every score below is from your stated premises, not from measurement.
- Whether a compliance, sovereignty, or customer-contract obligation already requires a non-S3 target — that would be a §8c floor and would change the verdict. Check with whoever owns your DPAs and hosting commitments.

```
Subject:        Proposed StorageProvider interface in front of the sole S3 client
Mode:           Prospective
Necessity:      Fail
Necessity note: §1a generality without instantiation — abstraction whose anticipated
                variation has not materialized; pattern-prerequisite check (§1b) fails,
                as port/strategy requires ≥2 implementations and there is one. §8a
                optionality premium does not apply: no named, probable second store.
Outcome evidence: none — no linked hypothesis; no vendor-switch requirement exists
Decision:       DROP (necessity failure)
Rationale:      The problem the interface solves — swapping storage vendors — cannot
                occur in the current stack because no second vendor is planned or
                requested, so day one ships an interface with one implementation.
                Worth scoring is skipped per §1/§6.1. The portability rationale is
                speculative optionality, which YAGNI rejects as the null hypothesis;
                the honest cost (indirection, duplicate vocabulary, lowest-common-
                denominator API suppressing presigned URLs, multipart, storage classes)
                is paid on every storage change until a second store exists.
Next action:    Use the AWS SDK directly; record the rejection with the structural
                rationale so it is not re-proposed without a named second store.
Verification:   Not run — no application code in this directory (only .claude/skills/).
                Closes with: rg -n "boto3|S3Client|@aws-sdk/client-s3|s3://" --stats
Minimal alt:    If and only if S3 details leak into domain logic across several modules,
                a thin domain-named module (store_upload / fetch_upload) over the SDK,
                with S3 types in its signatures and no vendor-neutrality claim. This is
                a separate candidate justified by call-site duplication, not portability.
Revisit when:   A second store is concretely named — signed contract, data-residency or
                compliance requirement, or an on-prem/air-gapped deployment target —
                or domain modules holding raw S3 types exceed a handful. Then extract
                the interface from the two real call patterns rather than designing it
                up front. (Not required for a necessity failure; the trigger is a change
                in the stack's invariants.)
```
